item.title: Re: 220% - Incorrect?
item.content:encoded:
There is something you all overlooked in this discussion: apparenlty, SCP-248 makes the subject opperate at EXACTLY 110%, that's why a half-destroyed tractor (which was, let's say, at 50% operation value), was able to work slightly better than 100%.
When applied to a fully functional computer, it also improved the ending value to 110%, so it is perfectly possible to conclude that the SCP makes the subject work at 110%, regardless of it's previous efficacy.
That would mean that adding another sticker from SCP-248 would do nothing, neither 121% nor 220%.

But that's just my two cents, I'm new here and I don't mean to cause any trouble.

EDIT: Plus, Chazz's got a point there, if the author says that 2 110% stickers add up to a 220% sticker, it should be so, and that's pretty much the end of it.

item.title: Re: 220% - Incorrect?

item.title: Re: 220% - Incorrect?
item.content:encoded: No, see, the original sticker makes it work at 110 percent. Which means, it's variable. Most things don't work at 100 percent effciency. So, if applied to something that is working at 110, it doubles it, because it can.

item.title: Re: 220% - Incorrect?
item.content:encoded: Not necessarily. The 110% sticker gives a 10% boost in efficiency (making the machine run at 110% efficiency). Putting a 110% sticker (+10% efficiency) on a machine running at 110% efficiency is 110% + 11% (10% of 110), which is 121%. I'm fairly certain that I'm right. The second sticker in the article gave a 110% boost, so that sticker would have to be a 210% sticker (roughly).

item.title: Re: 220% - Incorrect?
item.content:encoded:
My understanding from that would be that the numbers were cumulative, not the effects. So if the stickers all had different numbers than 110, and you affixed a 25%, 110%, and a 30%, the final total would be the same as putting on a 165%.

To put it in algebra turns, we're looking at (110*S)E, where the 110 is the percentage (obviously), S is the number of stickers, and E is the original efficiency of the object in question.

In order to achieve what you were suggesting, one would have to put a 110% sticker ON a 110% sticker, so the second one boosts the first one, which in turn boosts the object in question.

item.title: 220% - Incorrect?
item.content:encoded: If the first 110% sticker adds a 10% efficiency boost, then the second sticker should only boost the already-boosted item by another 10%. Meaning, an object with two stickers would operate at 121% efficiency, not 220%. I would change it myself, but I'm new. Overstepping bounds, and such.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
And that's what makes it so weird.

Alternately, how about 110% squared? 1.1^2 = 121%. The first sticker does 110% of the baseline performance, and the second sticker does 110% of the boosted level. Using the tractor again, the baseline would be 42km/h / 1.1 = 32.wholelotta18s km/h. Uh… anyway, if 42km/h is 110% of baseline, then 110% of boosted = 121% of baseline = 46.2 km/h, which is a bit more meh than 84 km/h.

I think the addition stacking of percentages is a bit more creepy than just regular multiplication. Why have a possible-to-overclock-without-248 121% of baseline when you can go all out and have 220%?

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Something about this was nagging at me, and I only realized what it was last night. When you put two of the things on a machine, its efficiency shoots up to 220%. The logic behind this is apparently 110% + 110% = 220%. I'm pretty damn sure you can't add percentages like that.
Say we have something operating at 4 units. Putting on one sticker would make it operate at 4.4 units, or 4*1.10.
And if you put a second sticker on, in current cannon it would make it go to 8.8 units, or 4*2.20.
However, if this is true, we have to accept that the second sticker made the machine go from 4.4 to 8.8, which is 200% rather then 110%.
Either this is intentional, and we have a Factory item behaving inconsistently, or someone didn't do the basic multiplication here.
